Casts a ray from the named pane's camera through the given pixel of that pane and returns the first surface it meets: {hit, position_mm {world, local}, normal, reference, node}. Pixels are the pane's own, top-left origin, in the size reported by width_px/height_px — the same frame a minerva_cad_snapshot of that pane has before any max_edge downscale. This is how a point on a picture becomes a number.

editor_name.description: Name of the CAD editor tab (as returned by minerva_list_editors).

view.description: Which pane the pixel is in. Default 'active'. In narrow layout only one pane renders, so a named pane is REFUSED with a reason rather than answered from the pane that happens to be showing — use 'active' there, as minerva_cad_snapshot requires.

px.description: [x, y] pixel in that pane, top-left origin.

tools.name: minerva_cad_material
tools.description: IS THE SOLID ACTUALLY HERE? Every other check measures your solid AGAINST something — interference, clearance, fasteners — and AIR VIOLATES NOTHING: a tray whose floor was subtracted away passes all three. This asks about the material itself, in the two forms a person asks it in. at_mm=[x,y,z] answers {inside, state (inside|on|outside), body (which solid of the part, "" in air), body_index, nearest_surface_mm, nearest_point_mm} — is there material at this world point, and how far is the nearest surface. from_mm=[x,y,z] with direction_mm=[dx,dy,dz] walks a ray and answers {segments:[{entry_mm, exit_mm, thickness_mm, entry_point_mm, exit_point_mm, body, body_index}], count, total_thickness_mm, started_inside, surface_crossings, unbounded} — every run of material along it, WITH ITS THICKNESS, so a ray down through an enclosure reports the skin and then the floor and a missing floor is one segment instead of two. Containment is read from the B-Rep with OCCT's solid classifier: no tessellation, no bounding box, and no parity count that a coincident-face seam could flip. Millimetres in the world frame of the evaluated solid. parts=[binding] probes each named binding on its own, like the check verbs. A measuring verb: refused with checked:false while the document buffer is ahead of the evaluation, and every reply carries source_version / buffer_version / evaluated_at / stale.

editor_name.description: Name of the CAD editor tab (as returned by minerva_list_editors).

at_mm.description: [x, y, z] world point — the point form. Give this OR from_mm, never both.

from_mm.description: [x, y, z] world point the ray starts at — the ray form, with direction_mm.

direction_mm.description: [dx, dy, dz] the way the ray points, e.g. [0, 0, -1] for straight down. Need not be a unit vector.

max_distance_mm.description: How far along the ray to walk, millimetres. Default 10000.

tolerance_mm.description: How close to a face counts as ON it rather than in or out. Default 1e-7.

parts.description: Probe each of these DSL bindings on its own instead of the document's render target; each is evaluated with that binding as its trailing expression.

tools.name: minerva_cad_snapshot_fit
tools.description: A snapshot FRAMED ON SOMETHING. minerva_cad_snapshot captures the pane as the owner left it — pulled back far enough to work in, so a 100 mm part fills a fifth of the frame and a grille hole is two pixels. This renders the SAME scene offscreen from a camera of its own, standing where `fit` fills the frame with a ~5% margin, and writes a PNG. The pane's camera is never moved: nothing the owner is looking at changes. fit='solid' frames the evaluated solid, fit='reference:<name>' one mounted reference (minerva_cad_references names them), fit=[[x0,y0,z0],[x1,y1,z1]] any world box in millimetres. Returns {path, absolute_path, width, height, fit_box_mm, view, view_preset, margin}; return_base64=true adds image_base64 (raw base64 PNG, no data: prefix) for direct vision consumption. ONLY A PANE ON PERSPECTIVE CAN BE FITTED — a pane looking from a direction draws its outline in the pane itself rather than in the world, so an offscreen render of it would be a different picture under its name, and it is refused with that reason; take an unfitted minerva_cad_snapshot of those. Refused too when nothing is being drawn at all (window occluded or minimised), because the fitted view needs a frame of its own; minerva_cad_snapshot reads the last frame the pane drew and needs none.

editor_name.description: Name of the CAD editor tab (as returned by minerva_list_editors).

view.description: Which pane to capture. Default 'active'. In narrow layout only one pane renders, so a named pane is REFUSED with a reason — use 'active' there.

fit.description: What to frame on: 'solid' (default), 'reference:<name>', or [[x0,y0,z0], [x1,y1,z1]] — two opposite corners of a world box in millimetres, either order.

margin.description: Air left around the box on the binding axis, as a fraction of it. Default 0.05; capped at 0.5.

max_edge.description: Clamp the long edge of the PNG to this many pixels (default 1024). Aspect ratio preserved.

output_path.description: Where to write the PNG. Default: user://cad_snapshots/fit_<view>_<timestamp>.png. Absolute, ~-prefixed or user:// accepted; res:// is rejected.

return_base64.description: If true, also include image_base64 (raw base64 PNG, no data: prefix).

tools.name: minerva_cad_snapshot_posed
tools.description: A picture FROM A PLACE YOU CHOOSE, and optionally CUT OPEN. Every other image verb reads the panes as the owner left them: minerva_cad_snapshot returns a fixed pane's last frame and minerva_cad_snapshot_fit reframes a pane without turning it, so nothing could look UNDER a part (three floorless STLs shipped because a missing floor is only visible from below). This renders the evaluated solid offscreen in a private world from the pose you state, framed on `fit` with the same meaning minerva_cad_snapshot_fit gives it, and writes a PNG. NO PANE IS INVOLVED: it needs no pane on Perspective, moves no camera the owner is using, and is NOT refused while the window is occluded or minimised (the frame is forced). Pose convention is the panes' own — yaw rotates about world +Z with yaw=0 on the +X side, pitch is degrees above the XY plane, and the pose is where the camera STANDS, so pitch=-90 is under the part looking up. section_plane={axis, offset_mm, keep} cuts the SOLID with a fragment discard so the interior is visible; mounted references are rendered whole, because a section is opened to see the solid around a reference. Returns {path, absolute_path, width, height, fit_box_mm, margin, pose{yaw_deg, pitch_deg, camera_position_mm, look_direction, target_mm, fov_deg}} — the pose is echoed even on a refusal — plus section_plane when one was asked for, and the eval freshness stamp (a render is stamped, never gated). return_base64=true adds image_base64 for direct vision consumption.

editor_name.description: Name of the CAD editor tab (as returned by minerva_list_editors).

view.description: Which DIRECTION to stand in — not which pane. '-z' is under the part looking up, '+z' is straight down, 'iso' is the iso pane's own three-quarter angle and 'iso-under' the same from below. Give this, or pose, or both (pose wins where they overlap).

pose.description: The camera pose. {yaw_deg, pitch_deg} place it on the sphere around the target: yaw about world +Z with 0 on the +X side, pitch degrees above the XY plane (-90 = directly underneath). distance_mm (optional) overrides how far back the fit would have put it; target_mm (optional) [x,y,z] is the point it aims at, default the centre of the fit box.

fit.description: What to frame on: 'solid' (default), 'reference:<name>', or [[x0,y0,z0], [x1,y1,z1]] — two opposite corners of a world box in millimetres, either order. Same meaning as in minerva_cad_snapshot_fit.

section_plane.description: Cut the solid open so the inside is visible. {axis: 'x'|'y'|'z', offset_mm: <where along that axis the cut is>, keep: '+' keeps the side above offset_mm, '-' the side below}. The cut is a fragment discard on the solid only; mounted references are rendered whole.

margin.description: Air left around the box on the binding axis, as a fraction of it. Default 0.05; capped at 0.5.

max_edge.description: Long edge of the PNG in pixels (default 1024); the render is 4:3.

output_path.description: Where to write the PNG. Default: user://cad_snapshots/posed_<timestamp>.png. Absolute, ~-prefixed or user:// accepted; res:// is rejected.

return_base64.description: If true, also include image_base64 (raw base64 PNG, no data: prefix).

tools.name: minerva_cad_view_overlay
tools.description: Draw a millimetre grid on the CAD floor and/or the three world axes through the origin, in every pane, and report each pane's scale: {px_per_mm, origin_px, width_px, height_px, projection, view_preset}. px_per_mm is a real number for a pane under an orthographic projection and null for one under perspective, which has no single scale. view_preset is the direction the pane is currently looking from (perspective/top/bottom/front/back/left/right): the pane ids are SLOTS on screen and keep their names, but the owner can point any pane anywhere from its own dropdown, so read view_preset rather than assuming 'top' looks down. The overlay is scene geometry, so the picture is still taken with minerva_cad_snapshot — call this first and the snapshot comes back with a ruler in it. overlay='none' clears it. In narrow layout the four named panes do not exist, so 'views' holds the one pane that renders and 'views_unavailable' says why the others are missing.

editor_name.description: Name of the CAD editor tab (as returned by minerva_list_editors).

grid_mm.description: Requested grid spacing in millimetres. Doubled as needed to keep the grid readable; the spacing actually drawn is returned. Default 10.

tools.name: minerva_cad_get_selected_reference
tools.description: What the user last pointed at on a reference mesh — the sibling of minerva_cad_get_selected_edge for foreign geometry. Returns {selected, reference, node, point_mm {world, local}, normal, bounds_mm {local, world}, size_mm, view, px, nearest_hole}. The click is the handoff: the user knows which bracket or which hole they mean and cannot say it in millimetres, so read this before measuring and you measure the thing they pointed at. point_mm.local is the reference's own converted frame — millimetres, Z-up, with the mesh() pose taken back off (what you write into the .mcad, because the pose is applied on top of it); point_mm.world is the posed scene. nearest_hole is the FITTED hole the point lies inside, if any — a hypothesis, not a measurement; minerva_cad_find_holes gauges it. stale=true means the document no longer mounts that reference, or — with a stale_reason beside it — that the document changed while this verb was waiting; call again.

editor_name.description: Name of the CAD editor tab (as returned by minerva_list_editors).

include_hole.description: Look for the fitted hole the selected point lies inside. Costs one segmentation pass on the first call for a file, cached afterwards. Default true.

tools.name: minerva_cad_select_reference
tools.description: Select a reference node from here, the way a user selects one by clicking it in a view: it highlights in the panel's reference list and becomes what minerva_cad_get_selected_reference returns. Use it to point at a node you found by name so the user can see which one you mean. With no point_mm the selection sits at the centre of the node's bounds; give point_mm (in the reference's own frame) to point at a specific spot. Returns the same payload as minerva_cad_get_selected_reference.

editor_name.description: Name of the CAD editor tab (as returned by minerva_list_editors).

reference.description: Reference name, as reported by minerva_cad_references.

node.description: Node inside that reference (references[].nodes[].name). Defaults to its first node.

point_mm.description: [x, y, z] in the REFERENCE's own frame, not the world. Optional.

include_hole.description: Look for the fitted hole the point lies inside. Default true.

tools.name: minerva_cad_view_state
tools.description: Read-only snapshot of what the user is currently looking at in a live CAD editor: the responsive layout class (xs/sm/md/lg/xl), the active viewport pane id (top/front/right/iso in wide layout, or the narrow-layout single pane), the narrow-layout projection dropdown selection, and the active pane camera's orientation/zoom (view_preset, target [x,y,z] in mm, distance, yaw, pitch). Use this for SEE-context before deciding whether a minerva_cad_snapshot is worth taking, or to confirm which pane a snapshot view="active" call would capture.

editor_name.description: Name of the CAD editor tab (as returned by minerva_list_editors).

tools.name: minerva_cad_await_eval
tools.description: Wait until the CAD panel's evaluation has SETTLED, and return the status it painted. An edit that reaches the panel through the shared text buffer — minerva_doc_edit on the text tab, or the user typing — starts a quarter-second debounce and then a worker round-trip, and neither has finished when the edit tool returns: a minerva_cad_get_mesh_info or check_* call made straight afterwards measures the geometry the edit REPLACED, with nothing in its reply to say so. Call this in between. Returns {timed_out, waited_ms, timeout_ms, last_eval:{status, ts, shape_name, body_count, vertex_count, edge_count, interference (a status line), banner, error_kind, error_message}}; status is empty / pending / ok / error / cancelled / timeout. 'banner' is the one line the panel is SHOWING the user — {visible, dismissed, stamp, eval, text} — stamped with the evaluation it came from; dismissed true means the user closed that report, which closes only that one: the next evaluation reports again. timed_out true is not a failure — the evaluation is still running, nothing was cancelled, and asking again resumes the wait. minerva_doc_write is already synchronous with the worker and does not need this. The reply carries source_version, buffer_version, evaluated_at and stale, so a caller can see in one field whether the panel has caught up with the document; the check verbs refuse to measure while it has not.

editor_name.description: Name of the CAD editor tab (as returned by minerva_list_editors).

timeout_ms.description: How long to wait, in milliseconds. Default 30000, capped at 300000. A timeout returns the status the panel is showing rather than an error.

skills.title: CAD modeling with the .mcad DSL
skills.summary: Author and edit .mcad parametric CAD documents (creating an anonymous editor on demand) — 2D sketches, 3D primitives, CSG, transforms, fillets/chamfers, modules — and use edge annotations to converse with the user about specific geometry. Reference meshes and measurement are in the companion skill minerva_cad_measuring.
skills.preconditions: A .mcad document is open OR the user has asked for CAD geometry (the agent can spawn an anonymous editor on demand via minerva_create_plugin_editor).
skills.outcome: The .mcad source produces the geometry the user described. Translator errors are surfaced verbatim. When the user needs to point at specific geometry, edges are labelled with annotations they can see in every viewport.
skills.steps:
0. If no CAD editor is open, call minerva_create_plugin_editor {plugin_id: "cad", editor_item_id: "new_mcad", tab_title: "<descriptive>"} to spawn an anonymous one. Use the returned editor_name as the key for steps 1–6. Ask the user to click the point BEFORE arming any annotation tool: while a tool is armed the annotation overlay captures every click and no reference point can be picked.
1. Read current source via minerva_doc_read keyed on editor_name (anonymous) or path (file-backed).
2. If geometry exists, call minerva_cad_get_mesh_info + minerva_cad_list_edges_live to ground edits in the current B-Rep.
3. When the user references edges they labeled ("the edges I pinned", "these edges"), call minerva_cad_list_user_labels FIRST and operate on every edge_id returned (multi-edge requests need ALL of them, not just the most-recent click). To ASK "which edge?", label candidates yourself with minerva_cad_annotate_edges; if the user clicks one, read minerva_cad_get_selected_edge.
4. Replace source with minerva_doc_write {editor_name, text: <full new source>}; the panel auto-evaluates and the reply carries last_eval. To change ONE line of a long document, minerva_doc_edit on the TEXT tab (the render tab refuses it) followed by minerva_cad_await_eval — that path is debounced, so the edit tool returns before the worker has answered.
4b. On a document with a mesh() in it, activate the skill minerva_cad_measuring — it carries mesh(), the measurement verbs and the loop to run after every write.
4c. To SEE the geometry rather than read it: minerva_cad_snapshot_fit {fit: "solid"} on a Perspective pane — the picture minerva_cad_snapshot takes, but framed on the part so it fills the frame instead of a fifth of it, and taken without moving the owner's camera. fit also accepts 'reference:<name>' or a world box [[x0,y0,z0],[x1,y1,z1]] in mm to look at one detail close up.
5. Clear stale labels with minerva_cad_clear_edge_annotations when the topic changes.
6. Save with minerva_doc_save when the user confirms; pass `path` on the first save of an anonymous editor (Save-As renames the tab — use the returned editor_name afterwards).
skills.system_prompt:
§0 — MCAD vs OpenSCAD habits (read FIRST)

MCAD looks like OpenSCAD but is not OpenSCAD. The worker DOES accept cylinder(h=, r=, center=true) and the boolean operators &&, ||, !. It DOES NOT accept //, /* */, trailing semicolons, sphere(d=), or OpenSCAD union() {...} blocks.

OpenSCAD habits to drop:
- // and /* */ comments → use # only.
- ; at end of statements → never. One statement per line.
- sphere(d=10) → use sphere(5) (radius). No diameter keyword.
- union() { a; b; } / difference() { a - b; } → use a + b and a - b operators.
- module foo() { return shape; } with braces → Python-ish module foo(): ... return shape.

If you find yourself writing //, ;, sphere(d=, or a { — STOP. Re-read §1.

§1 — DSL vocabulary (vetted against canonical .mcad examples)

.mcad is indentation-aware (Python-style). The build123d/OCCT worker evaluates it into a B-Rep solid plus an indexed edge registry.

The evaluated result is the last 3D binding the program assigns, UNLESS the final line is a bare expression (`enclosure` alone on the last line), which selects that shape instead — snapshot, list_edges, get_mesh_info, export and the checks all follow the selection, and a trailing expression that is not a solid is a translate error.

Variables and arithmetic:
  height = 100
  width = 80
  thickness = 10

2D primitives — used inside `sketch:` blocks, and ONLY there:
  rect(w, h)
  circle(r)
  oval(w, h)
That is the whole 2D vocabulary. There is no polygon() — an arbitrary outline is built by adding and subtracting these inside the sketch, and an arbitrary SOLID is polyhedron(points=..., faces=...), which is 3D and is refused inside sketch:. A loft: section is a 2D profile expression built from the same three.

3D primitives:
  cube(x, y, z)                                # axis-aligned box, CORNER AT ORIGIN — extents [0,0,0]→[x,y,z]. To centre: translate([-x/2,-y/2,-z/2], cube(x,y,z))
  sphere(r)                                    # radius — no d= keyword. CENTRED at origin.
  cylinder(r, h)                               # positional. Axis along +Z. Without center=true the base sits at z=0 and the top at z=h.
  cylinder(h=H, r=R, center=true)              # keyword form (canonical examples use this when translating/rotating cylinders)
  cylinder(h=H, r1=BIG, r2=SMALL, center=true) # truncated cone

CSG operators:
  a + b   # union (fuse)
  a - b   # difference (cut)
No * intersection operator.

Transforms — function form with array vector:
  translate([x, y, z], shape)
  rotate([rx, ry, rz], shape)   # degrees about each axis
  scale([sx, sy, sz], shape)
  mirror([nx, ny, nz], shape)

Reference meshes — a foreign file placed in the scene, never altered (see §12):
  board = mesh("boards/main.glb")                     # path recorded verbatim; the panel resolves it against the .mcad file
  board = translate([0, 0, 5], rotate([0, 0, 90], mesh("main.glb")))
  part  = mesh("scan.stl", units="mm", up="z")        # units/up override the format default

2D positioning sugar inside sketch: blocks:
  rect(w, h) center at point(x, y)

Operations:
  extrude(profile, length)
  fillet shape, [<edge_idx>, ...], r=R    # PREFERRED: list form. All ids resolved against the current registry, applied in ONE OCCT op.
  fillet shape, <edge_idx>, r=R           # single-edge form. SAFE only as a one-off — see §11 before chaining.
  chamfer shape, [<edge_idx>, ...], d=D   # PREFERRED list form (note: distance keyword is `d=`, not `c=`).
  chamfer shape, <edge_idx>, d=D          # single-edge form. Same caveat as fillet.
  shell shape, thickness               # postfix; mutates `shape` in place
  loft:                                # block — see §2
      z=N: profile_expr
      ...

Export:
  export name "filename.{stl|3mf|step|glb}"

§2 — Language constructs

`sketch:` blocks are ANONYMOUS. Bind named 2D shapes inside, combine with +/-, then `extrude` references the inner variable by name:

  sketch:
      flange = rect(width, thickness) center at point(0, height - thickness / 2)
      web    = rect(thickness, height - thickness) center at point(0, (height - thickness) / 2)
      profile = flange + web

  beam = extrude(profile, length)

CRITICAL: do NOT write `sketch <name>:` — sketches don't take a name. Do NOT put bare `rect(...)` lines without `name = rect(...)` — the block needs named profiles to compose.

`for` loops over a list:
  for p in [[-25, 95, 25], [25, 95, 25], [-25, 95, 175], [25, 95, 175]]:
      beam = beam - translate(p, slug)

`while` (use sparingly — worker has an iteration cap):
  while count < hole_n:
      ...
      count = count + 1

`if` / `else` with boolean operators &&, ||, !:
  if z > half_len && count != 0:
      beam = beam - translate([0, 95, z], big_slug)
  else:
      beam = beam - translate([0, 95, z], small_slug)

`module` — reusable parameterised geometry; MUST end with `return <shape>`:
  module hole_slug(bolt_r, csink_r, depth=10):
      through = rotate([90, 0, 0], cylinder(h=depth + 4, r=bolt_r, center=true))
      csink   = translate([0, depth/2 - 2, 0], rotate([90, 0, 0], cylinder(h=5, r1=csink_r, r2=bolt_r, center=true)))
      return through + csink

  slug = hole_slug(4, 7)

`loft:` block — sections at successive Z planes:
  body = loft:
      z=0:   oval(58, 34)
      z=40:  oval(66, 40)
      z=78:  oval(60, 36)
      z=110: oval(34, 18)

Indentation rule: a colon-terminated header (for, if, else, while, module, sketch, loft) starts an indented block. Don't mix tabs and spaces.

§3 — Viewports & coordinate frame

The CAD panel is Z-UP (matching build123d / FreeCAD / SolidWorks native frames): +X is right, +Y is depth (into the screen in iso), +Z is up. The default cylinder() axis is +Z, so a cylinder's "top end" sits at +Z. The default sketch plane is XY (floor), and `extrude(profile, length)` extrudes along +Z — meaning a sketch+extrude T-beam stands on its END with length vertical. That's not a bug, it's the build123d sketch-plane convention being explicit: use it intentionally, and consider rotate([90,0,0], extrude(...)) if you want a horizontal beam.

Wide layout (md/lg/xl) is a 2×2 grid: top/front/right (orthographic OUTLINE x-ray — not shaded 3D renders) + iso (shaded). Narrow layout has ONE switchable view via the projection dropdown. Pane semantics:
- Top   : looks down -Z onto the XY plane. Holes through a cube along +Z appear as CIRCLES here. X right, Y up on screen.
- Front : looks toward +Y from -Y; the XZ plane fills the view. X right, Z up on screen.
- Right : looks toward -X from +X; the YZ plane fills the view. Y right, Z up on screen.
- Iso   : orbited perspective, Z up.

Trust iso for "did the geometry build right," ortho for dimensions/symmetry. When you say "top of the part" to the user, you mean +Z.

§4 — Talking via edge annotations (USER → agent first)

Every evaluated solid has stable indexed edges, and there are TWO label channels:

A. User-authored labels (the user clicks edges in the panel and types notes)
   When the user references "the edges I labeled" (or "pinned"/"tagged"/"marked"/"selected"), they mean these. Call minerva_cad_list_user_labels FIRST. It returns {labels: [{edge_id, text, ...}], count}. Operate on every edge_id in the list — do NOT rely on minerva_cad_get_selected_edge (that returns ONLY the most recent click, not the whole set the user has been pinning). If count==0, then the user has not labeled anything; fall back to get_selected_edge or ask which edges they mean.

B. Agent-authored labels (you label edges so the user can answer "which one?")
   When you and the user need to disambiguate edges, call minerva_cad_list_edges_live, pick candidates, label with minerva_cad_annotate_edges using readable labels ("A", "B", "C"), and ask. The user may then click an edge — read minerva_cad_get_selected_edge for that single click. Clear stale labels with minerva_cad_clear_edge_annotations before the next set.

Edge indices from either channel feed fillet/chamfer in the DSL directly.

§5 — Starting from scratch

No editor open? Spawn one:
  minerva_create_plugin_editor {plugin_id: "cad", editor_item_id: "new_mcad", tab_title: "<descriptive>"}

Returns {editor_name, text_editor_name, buffer_path}. The render panel and the text editor share one DocumentBuffer — passing either name to minerva_doc_* hits the same buffer. No file path until Save-As.

To author or rewrite source:
- minerva_doc_write {editor_name, text: "<full new .mcad source>"}
minerva_doc_edit (string replace) is REFUSED on the render tab ("plugin_scene_unsupported") but works on the paired TEXT tab, and is the cheap way to change one line of a long document — see §6 for it, and for the wait it needs.

To read source:
- minerva_doc_read {editor_name} → {text, last_eval, ...}.

To save:
- First save (anonymous → disk): minerva_doc_save {editor_name, path: "<full path>"}.
- After binding: minerva_doc_save {editor_name}.

§6 — Verifying success (automatic, no polling)

A CAD document has TWO tabs: the text tab (the .mcad source) and the render tab (the panel). minerva_doc_write on either is SYNCHRONOUS with the worker eval — the tool reply already contains last_eval populated. Read last_eval.status from the doc_write reply:

- ok        — geometry rendered. last_eval has shape_name, body_count, vertex_count, edge_count, etc. Tell the user what you built. body_count > 1 means the part is several separate solids: right for a two-half enclosure, and a sign something fell off the union when you expected one.
- error     — worker rejected the DSL. The MCP reply has success=false; surface last_eval.error_kind and last_eval.error_message verbatim. error_kind is parse (a lex or syntax error; the message carries line and column), translate (well-formed DSL, impossible operation) or occt (the geometry kernel failed — the message NAMES the binding that was building or being tessellated, and last_eval.error_frame is the innermost kernel frame), or python (an exception that did not come from the kernel, raised while that binding was building — it still names the binding and the line, but the fault is not geometry). Common causes: OpenSCAD habits (§0), unknown identifiers, sketch block missing variable bindings, indentation drift. On kind occt edit the named binding first; the raw cad.evaluate reply carries the whole traceback as error.traceback and, for a tessellation failure, error.details.untriangulated_faces with the coordinates of the faces that defeated it.
- timeout   — the panel gave up waiting. It waits 15 minutes, and last_eval.elapsed_ms says how long it actually waited; a heavy document answers long before that, so this status means the worker never answered at all. Suggest simplifying.
- cancelled — preempted by a newer evaluate (rare).
- empty     — source was whitespace-only.

NEVER tell the user "done" without reading last_eval.status. The reply is the canonical truth.

last_eval is a STATUS, not a report. It carries shape_name, body_count, vertex_count, edge_count, mesh_defects, mesh_defect_sites, and interference as a summary line (checked, count, point_count and the nodes met). The crossing points come from minerva_cad_check_interference and the reference rows from minerva_cad_references; both re-ask the question against the geometry standing now, which is what you want anyway. mesh_defect_sites is where the defects ARE: non-manifold edges as world positions with their two endpoints (up to 64 sites spread across the part, with the total beside them) (three or more faces meet there — a slicer cannot read it, so fix the feature nearest that point), and a capped spread sample of degenerate faces. Degenerate counts include tessellation slivers on curved faces and are NOT defects by themselves; non-manifold edges are.

EDITING WITHOUT RE-SENDING THE WHOLE FILE. minerva_doc_edit (string replace) works on the TEXT tab of a paired CAD document — it is a plain text buffer — and is the cheap way to change one dimension in a long document. It is refused on the RENDER tab ("plugin_scene_unsupported"), which is a structured document. But it is NOT synchronous: the edit starts a quarter-second debounce and then the worker round-trip, so the tool returns before any of it has happened. Call minerva_cad_await_eval {editor_name} straight after: it returns when the panel has painted, with the same last_eval, and a timed_out reply means the evaluation is still running (nothing was cancelled — ask again). A check_* or get_mesh_info call made without that wait measures the geometry the edit replaced.

CHEAP EVALUATION. minerva_cad_cad_evaluate with summary=true evaluates source and returns {shape_name, body_count, bbox, vertex_count, face_count, edge_count, reference_count, mesh_defects} with NO mesh — the cheap "does this compile, and how big is it" call. The full reply carries every vertex.

Cold-start note: the first eval after Minerva starts can take ~10s (worker process spinup). Don't worry if a single doc_write seems slow — subsequent calls are fast.

Ground before authoring. When you're about to subtract holes/features from existing geometry — or you're combining primitives whose origin conventions might not all match — call minerva_cad_get_mesh_info FIRST and read the bounding_box. The bbox is the single source of truth for "where is the part?" and "what are its extents?". Place children with bbox.min and bbox.max as anchors, not assumed-symmetric coords like [-x/2, x/2]. The cube() corner-at-origin convention bites this exact pattern: a cube(25,25,25) sits in [0,0,0]→[25,25,25], so a hole grid centered around the origin will MISS most of the cube.

§7 — Worked examples (canonical — these are known to evaluate)

10 mm-diameter sphere:
  result = sphere(5)

T-beam (extruded structural section):
  height = 100
  width = 80
  thickness = 10
  length = 100

  sketch:
      flange = rect(width, thickness) center at point(0, height - thickness / 2)
      web    = rect(thickness, height - thickness) center at point(0, (height - thickness) / 2)
      profile = flange + web

  beam = extrude(profile, length)

T-beam with countersunk holes (module + for + CSG subtraction):
  height = 100
  width = 80
  thickness = 10
  length = 200

  sketch:
      flange = rect(width, thickness) center at point(0, height - thickness / 2)
      web    = rect(thickness, height - thickness) center at point(0, (height - thickness) / 2)
      profile = flange + web

  beam = extrude(profile, length)

  module hole_slug(bolt_r, csink_r, depth=10):
      through = rotate([90, 0, 0], cylinder(h=depth + 4, r=bolt_r, center=true))
      csink   = translate([0, depth/2 - 2, 0], rotate([90, 0, 0], cylinder(h=5, r1=csink_r, r2=bolt_r, center=true)))
      return through + csink

  slug = hole_slug(4, 7)

  for p in [[-25, 95, 25], [25, 95, 25], [-25, 95, 175], [25, 95, 175]]:
      beam = beam - translate(p, slug)

Lofted shell body (organic profile + shell op):
  body = loft:
      z=0:   oval(58, 34)
      z=40:  oval(66, 40)
      z=78:  oval(60, 36)
      z=110: oval(34, 18)

  shell body, 1.8

When the user asks for something close to one of these, START by adapting the matching example — don't synthesise from scratch. Confirm the build via §6, then iterate.

§8 — Exporting to STL / STEP / 3MF / GLB

Use minerva_cad_export {editor_name, format, path} to write the current model to disk. The tool resolves the editor's source via DocumentRegistry — you do NOT need to read or pass the source yourself. Source the panel has already evaluated is exported from the part that evaluation built (reused_evaluation true) and costs only the file write; source that has not been evaluated is built from scratch, which is where the "still building" answer below comes from.

Formats:
- 'stl'       → binary STL (build123d default; ASCII is not exposed). Best for slicers, mesh consumers.
- 'step' / 'stp' → STEP AP214 (OCCT default schema). Best for handing off to other CAD tools (Fusion, SolidWorks, FreeCAD).
- '3mf'       → 3MF via build123d Mesher. Modern slicer format, units + colour aware. The writer VALIDATES first: 3MF takes only a closed manifold solid, so a part with non-manifold edges or degenerate/duplicate faces is refused with kind=mesh_invalid, and the message names the defect class, its count and the part. Those counts are last_eval.mesh_defects (§6) — read them there. Their positions are last_eval.mesh_defect_sites, and the refusal repeats both. Fix the geometry, or export 'stl'/'step', which accept the part as it stands.
- 'glb'       → minimal binary glTF: one mesh, one node named after the part. Written in the glTF frame (metres, Y-up), which is what mesh() assumes for a .glb, so exporting a DSL stand-in and mounting it back with mesh("that.glb") — no units=/up= needed — lands it at the same size and pose. This is the round trip for off-board stand-ins.

Path rules: absolute as-is; ~-prefixed paths expand; bare relative paths resolve against the user's home directory.

AN EXPORT THAT MUST BUILD RUNS DETACHED. If it is still building after about 20 s the verb answers kind=running with elapsed_ms — and the host currently surfaces that as {success: false, error: 'cad_export_failed (kind=running): ...'}. That is NOT a failure: nothing has been written, nothing has been cancelled, and the build carries on. Call minerva_cad_export AGAIN with the same editor, format and path to collect the file when it lands. On a large lofted shell that can be minutes; do not rewrite the source or tell the user the export failed.

Return shape on success: {success: true, path, bytes_written, format}. Surface the path back to the user verbatim — they may want to grab the file. On a parse/translate error the tool returns {success: false, error: 'cad_export_failed (kind=parse|translate): ...'} with the worker's verbatim message; treat it the same way you treat doc_write last_eval errors (§6). A 3MF refusal comes back the same way with kind=mesh_invalid; surface the defect class and count it names — that is the geometry to fix, not the exporter.

Do NOT use the DSL `export <name> "file.stl"` statement — it parses cleanly but the worker does not flush export targets during cad.evaluate. minerva_cad_export is the only path that actually writes a file.

§9 — Visual verification: minerva_cad_snapshot

TRIGGER: When the user complains about how the model LOOKS ("that's not right", "the chamfers all look the same", "holes are off", "can't tell", "still wrong" — ANY visual comment), your FIRST action is minerva_cad_snapshot, NOT minerva_doc_write. You cannot fix a visual problem you cannot see. Bumping constants without seeing the result wastes the user's time and almost always produces another visually-identical wrong answer.

If you have vision capability, call minerva_cad_snapshot {editor_name, view?: "iso"|"top"|"front"|"right"|"active", return_base64?: true} to SEE the model. Use this any time text-only inspection (mesh_info, list_edges) won't disambiguate what went wrong — e.g. "are the holes on the cube or floating off it?", "do the chamfers look different from each other?". Set return_base64=true to receive the PNG inline; otherwise the tool writes to disk under user://cad_snapshots/ and you get the path back.

Narrow vs wide layout: in NARROW layout only the visible single pane is rendering, so view="top"/"front"/"right" while the projection dropdown is on something else returns null with kind "not rendering". Use view="active" (whatever pane is currently shown), or ask the user to switch the panel to wide layout. The tool internally awaits one frame_post_draw, so cold-start nulls no longer reach you — if you DO get a non-cold-start null error, retrying with the same view will NOT help.

Do NOT retry minerva_cad_snapshot with identical args after a not-rendering failure. The system warns after 3 identical failures; treat that warning as a hard stop. Tell the user what you can't see and propose either switching layout or interpreting the geometry numerically (mesh_info bbox, list_edges).

§10 — Reading the user's intent precisely

CAD asks are often ambiguous in ways that produce visually identical wrong answers. Two patterns bite repeatedly:

(a) QUANTIFIER AMBIGUITY. "Give each hole a larger chamfer" has two readings:
  - Reading A: every hole gets a (uniform) chamfer that is larger than baseline.
  - Reading B: each hole gets a DIFFERENT chamfer, varying across the grid.
Reading B is signalled by words like "each", "different", "varied", "vary", "a gradient of", "per-hole". Reading A is signalled by "all the holes", "uniformly", "a bigger chamfer overall". When ambiguous, STATE YOUR READING in your reply: "I'm reading this as a uniform chamfer increase — every hole gets the same larger size. If you meant varying chamfers per hole, say so and I'll parameterise the module on chamfer_r."

Reading B requires the per-iteration variable to actually VARY. A module called once and translated to many positions produces identical-shape copies — translation is rigid, it does not reshape. To get per-iteration variation you must either: (i) make the module take args and call it with different values per position, or (ii) compute per-iteration values inline.

(b) PUSHBACK ESCALATION. If the user says the result "looks the same", "is still wrong", "didn't change", "all look identical" — DO NOT just bump the same constants and rewrite. That is the failure mode: three tiny edits that all evaluate cleanly and look identical because the underlying ambiguity was never resolved.

When pushed back on a visual result, do EXACTLY ONE of:
  1. Snapshot first (§9) to see what they are seeing. If the snapshot confirms the issue, the geometry is wrong; reason about WHY before rewriting.
  2. Ask which reading they meant. "Do you want them all the same size but bigger, or each hole a DIFFERENT size?" One sentence.

If you find yourself about to call minerva_doc_write a second time after a visual complaint, with the same module structure and slightly different constants — STOP. You are in the failure mode. Snapshot or ask first.

§11 — fillet/chamfer: ALWAYS batch, NEVER chain

OCCT (the B-Rep kernel under build123d) does NOT have stable edge identifiers across topology changes. Every `fillet` and `chamfer` operation deletes the original sharp edge and adds new arc edges; OCCT's internal edge table is rebuilt and `shape.edges()` returns edges in a different order. The MCAD edge registry is just `1..N` over that traversal — so after a single fillet, every other edge id has shifted.

Consequence: writing four sequential fillet statements applies the FIRST fillet to the right edge, but the second/third/fourth statements reference ids that no longer mean what you intended. You will silently fillet the wrong edges (often top edges instead of vertical corners). The DSL evaluates cleanly, the geometry is wrong, and the user has to spot it visually.

ALWAYS use the list form when filleting or chamfering more than one edge:

  fillet  part, [1, 3, 6, 20], r=2
  chamfer part, [4, 8, 12, 16], d=0.5

Both list-form variants resolve ALL ids against the same pre-fillet registry, then call OCCT once. Stable IDs from start to finish.

If you find yourself about to emit a second `fillet` (or `chamfer`) statement on the SAME shape in the SAME doc_write — STOP. Combine the edge ids into a single list. The single-edge form exists only for the genuine one-off case (single corner, single edge); using it more than once per shape per doc_write is a bug.

(Edge ids are still unstable across SEPARATE doc_write calls — between calls the worker re-evaluates from scratch. Always re-list edges via minerva_cad_list_edges_live before each new authoring turn; never reuse ids from a previous turn.)

§12 — Reference meshes and measurement live in a second skill

`mesh()` — placing a board, a scan or a bought part in the scene — and every verb that MEASURES one (references, find_holes, find_cylinders, gauge, probe, check_interference, check_clearance, check_fasteners, the selection verbs) are described by the skill `minerva_cad_measuring`. Activate it the moment the document has a mesh() line in it, or the user asks you to fit anything to real geometry. Everything above still applies: the DSL, the edit loop and the verification rules are the same.

skills.title: Measuring reference meshes in CAD
skills.summary: Place foreign geometry in a .mcad document with mesh() and MEASURE it: holes and cylinders gauged rather than guessed, interference, clearance and fastener checks against the evaluated solid, part-against-part clearance and a height profile over a footprint (together, as one verdict, via minerva_cad_check_design), and the user's click as the seed for "this one".
skills.preconditions: A .mcad document is open and has a mesh() reference in it, or is about to get one. The DSL itself is described by the skill minerva_cad_modeling.
skills.outcome: Every number quoted to the user came from a gauge or a check rather than from a fit alone, in the frame that was asked about, and no edit was called done before interference, clearance and the fastener check had run.
skills.steps:
0. minerva_cad_references — what is mounted (lean by default; detail="full" for poses and per-node boxes; emit_dsl=true with clearance_mm writes those boxes back as keepout_<reference> envelopes to subtract).
1. minerva_cad_find_holes / minerva_cad_find_cylinders — the census, measured. emit_dsl=true writes the centres back as .mcad.
2. After every write on a document with a mesh() in it: read last_eval.interference (a summary, free), then minerva_cad_check_design {required_mm, screw?, expected_contacts} — one call that runs interference, fasteners and clearance in turn and answers with a verdict and only the failing rows. Declare the contacts the design MEANS to have in expected_contacts; an assembly whose declared contacts OVERLAP reads 'advisory' rather than 'pass' (the depth evidence is a chord, not a proof) — report it as advisory with pass_reason (its rows are under uncertified_rows, apart from failing_rows), and fix the worst row, write, check again. With parts=, a part still measuring is a ticket under tickets.clearance: collect it with minerva_cad_check_clearance ticket=, not with check_design. Call minerva_cad_check_clearance / _check_interference / _check_fasteners on their own for the rows check_design counted in hidden_counts but did not show.
2b. Laying parts out (off-board parts on a board, a stack inside a shell): minerva_cad_check_clearance {reference, against, required_mm} — or reference="all-pairs" — measures the references against EACH OTHER, and minerva_cad_reference_profile {region_mm} says how tall they are over a footprint. Both read the triangles; never answer either question from the boxes in minerva_cad_references.
3. minerva_cad_gauge for a direct "will this pin go in here", minerva_cad_probe to turn a pixel into millimetres.
3b. minerva_cad_snapshot_fit {fit: 'reference:<name>'} to LOOK at one mounted part close up — an offscreen render framed on it, taken without moving the pane. Perspective panes only.
3c. minerva_cad_material {at_mm} / {from_mm, direction_mm} — is the solid THERE at all. The three checks measure against references and air violates none of them, so a missing floor or a wall a boolean ate passes them; probe a point inside the wall you meant to build, or walk a ray through the part and read the thicknesses.
4. minerva_cad_get_selected_reference when the user says "this one".
skills.system_prompt:
§1 — What this skill is

Measuring FOREIGN geometry in a .mcad document: the mesh() primitive that puts it in the scene, and the verbs that answer questions about it in millimetres. The DSL itself, the edit loop and the fillet rules are in `minerva_cad_modeling` — activate that one too when you are also authoring geometry.

§2 — Reference meshes: mesh()

`mesh("path")` places an existing mesh file (.glb/.gltf and .stl; .obj as it lands) in the CAD world as REFERENCE geometry. It is a pose, not a solid:

- The worker never opens the file. It records the path exactly as you wrote it, the units and up-axis, and the composed 4x4 transform. The panel resolves the path relative to the saved .mcad document and loads it.
- translate / rotate / scale / mirror compose onto a reference in statement order, exactly as they do on a solid. scale() on a reference must be UNIFORM and non-zero — scale([2,2,2], ...) is fine, scale([1,2,1], ...) is an error naming the reference — because a non-uniform scale turns the file's holes into ellipses, which have no diameter for a measurement to report. translate([10,0,0], rotate([0,0,90], mesh("a.glb"))) is NOT the same placement as rotate([0,0,90], translate([10,0,0], mesh("a.glb"))).
- Nothing else may touch it. a - mesh(...), a + mesh(...), fillet, chamfer, shell, extrude, loft and export on a reference are all errors that name the reference. You cannot cut a solid against a reference, and you cannot reverse a mesh into DSL. If the user asks for either, say so plainly rather than emitting DSL that fails.
- Bind it to a name. Only a named top-level binding is reported to the panel: write board = mesh("main.glb"), never a bare mesh("main.glb") line.
- A reference contributes NO edges. Edge ids still come only from the B-Rep solids, so adding a mesh() line never renumbers the ids you got from minerva_cad_list_edges_live.
- Units and up default by format, because the formats differ: .glb/.gltf default to units="m", up="y" (the glTF spec's own frame); every other extension defaults to units="mm", up="z". Pass units= (mm/cm/m/in) and up= (x/y/z) only when you know the file disagrees with its format's convention.
- An STL says nothing about its own scale, so a .stl loaded without units= is read as millimetres AND warned about in the reply. A file authored in inches and mounted silently is 25.4x too big, and every clearance measured against it is wrong — write units= on every .stl line.

A document may contain nothing but references — that evaluates cleanly with an empty B-Rep, so importing a board before modelling anything around it is normal.

The owner has a GUI route to the same line: "Import mesh…" in the CAD panel opens a file picker filtered to the loadable formats and appends one refN = mesh("...") line to the document, spelled relative to the saved .mcad. There is no import tool for you, and none is coming: your parity for that action is minerva_doc_write on the same document — append the line yourself, in the same form. In a document that has never been saved the path has to be absolute (the panel warns about it); tell the user to save the .mcad beside the mesh if the pair has to travel.

§3 — Measuring a reference mesh: hypothesise, then verify

A reference is FOREIGN geometry. Nothing tells you where its holes are, and a picture of it will not tell you either — pixels are not millimetres. The measurement verbs give you numbers, and they are built around one rule: a fit is a hypothesis, a gauge is a measurement.

The workflow, in order:
1. minerva_cad_references — what is mounted, where it is posed, what its nodes bound. Start here; it is cheap and it names the references and nodes the other verbs take. It answers LEAN by default (name, status, world bounding box, node count); pass detail="full" when you need the pose, both frames or the per-node boxes, and reference=<name> to ask about one of them. On a forty-five node board the full listing is sixteen kilobytes and the lean one is a fraction of it — ask for full once, not five times. It also WRITES those boxes back: emit_dsl=true with clearance_mm=C returns .mcad in `dsl` binding one keepout_<reference> per reference — the union of one cube per node, each the node's WORLD box grown by C on every side — so a shell is written as `top = top - keepout_board - keepout_esp` instead of against four retyped numbers. nodes=[...] scopes it to the nodes you care about, and is REQUIRED above 200 nodes; dsl_omitted names anything left out. The cube is the WORLD box, so a part mounted at an angle keeps more air than it needs: the safe direction for a keep-out, the wrong direction for a skin height.
2. minerva_cad_find_holes — every hole, measured. Pass emit_dsl=true and the reply carries the census as .mcad in `dsl`: a slug per radius and axis, a translate() per hole at its world centre, ready to subtract (dsl_kind="post" adds standoffs at the same centres instead; dsl_clearance_mm widens every radius). Paste that rather than retyping four centres — dsl_skipped names any hole whose axis is not square to a world axis, which is the only case it will not write. Read dia_mm AND gauge_dia_mm: dia_mm is the circle the tessellation's vertices lie on (the drill the designer asked for), gauge_dia_mm is the largest pin the gauge's rays allow (the chord across the facets, always slightly smaller — a 3.2 mm drill exported as a 64-gon gauges 3.18). Read gauge_bounded: false means no wall was found inside the search bound, so gauge_dia_at_least_mm is a floor and there is no measured diameter. Quote the one the question is about, and say which it is. Read `through` before saying a hole goes through: a blind pocket has exactly the same wall as a through hole and only the ray test tells them apart. Read `verified`: false means the fit was not confirmed by the gauge and the number is a guess.
3. minerva_cad_find_cylinders kind=convex — bosses, standoffs and pins, the same way.
4. minerva_cad_gauge — the direct question: will THIS pin, at THIS place, go in? A gauge that does not fit tells you where it touched, which is the answer to 'why will this screw not go in'. Every gauge and every hole verification is RAY-SAMPLED — 24 azimuths at each of 5 stations along the pin — not a volumetric proof, so 'it fits' means no ray met anything: a rib, a burr or a chamfer standing between two rays can be missed (15° of arc is 1.3 mm of wall at a 5 mm radius). Say 'gauged, not proven' when the answer matters, and gauge again at a size or a place that would catch what you doubt. When the pin stands in open air nothing bounds it: the reply says clearance_bounded false and reports clearance_at_least_mm, which is the search bound and not a distance to anything.
4b. minerva_cad_check_interference — does what you just built RUN INTO any of it? You do not have to ask: every evaluation carries a SUMMARY of it in last_eval.interference (checked, count, point_count and the nodes met), and the panel draws red crosses at the crossing points. Call the verb for the points themselves — they are not in last_eval. last_eval.banner is that same summary as the USER sees it, one stamped line along the bottom of the panel: visible/dismissed says whether they have it in front of them or closed it, and a closed report closes only that evaluation's. READ IT after every doc_write on a document with a mesh() in it — count > 0 means your shell is inside the board, and the pair names the node and the depth. checked: false with a reason means the check could not run and is not a clean bill of health. Call the verb to re-ask after an edit or to scope it with reference=/node=. The check is complete for closed meshes, and a flush contact within 0.0001 mm is reported as touching rather than as interference, so a lid sitting ON a board is clean, and so is a bored boss seated on one: the mouth of a pilot in the seating face is not a penetration. The reply's `pass` is count 0 with nothing undecidable, and expected_contacts (4e) is how you make it reachable on an assembly.
4c. minerva_cad_check_clearance {required_mm} — by how much do you MISS? Interference answers whether two bodies touch; this answers how much air is between them, which is the number you edit a wall by. Ask it whenever a fit matters: a connector that has to clear a shell, a boss that has to miss a trace. The distance is exact for the two meshes and the reply carries the two points that realise it, so you know where the pinch is. ALWAYS quote tessellation_tolerance_mm alongside min_mm — the solid is a B-Rep measured through its tessellation, so the true clearance is at least min_mm minus that deviation; a clearance stated without it is not a measurement. min_mm 0 with interference true means there is no gap at all. A distance is UNSIGNED, so a node buried inside your solid would measure as a positive gap: the reply joins the latest interference report for the same source and reports any node it names at 0, failing. Read interference_join — when it says no report described this source, evaluate first. On a board with fifty pairs the report is twenty kilobytes: pass failing_only=true to drop the pairs that cleared the gap they had to keep, and limit=N to keep the N CLOSEST of what is left (they are sorted closest-first). failing_only keeps every row whose `pass` is false on a solid whose tolerance IS bounded (a certified failure is never hidden), and on one whose tolerance is not — tolerance_bounded false, where every row reads pass false — it is graded on the DISTANCE instead, so the filter still leaves only the real misses. A loft's or a sweep's spline flanks are measured by SAMPLING their curvature, which chooses a good chord step but proves nothing about the cell the grid stepped over, so such a solid reports tolerance_bounded false with tolerance_source 'sampled': its distances are advisory (accept_unbounded_tolerance grades them on min_mm) and never a certified pass. Neither changes the verdict — `pass` is graded over every pair, and pairs_total/pairs_shown/pairs_hidden always say what you did not see. Unlike 4b this one is not carried by every evaluation — you have to ask. On an assembled design, declare what is meant to touch (4e) or the verdict is noise.
4f. PART AGAINST PART, and how tall it is. Both checks above measure your solid against the references. Laying parts out is the other question — does the OLED sit on the devkit, does the joystick clear the connector — and it is asked with the SAME verbs: minerva_cad_check_clearance {reference, against, required_mm} measures two mounted references against each other, reference="all-pairs" measures every pair, and minerva_cad_check_interference with against= lists only the pairs with no air between them, with the points where they meet. Nothing is tessellated on this path, so there is no tessellation tolerance to quote: the distance is exact for the two meshes and the only error bar is quantization_mm. It measures NODE against node, and only the closest max_pairs candidates (200 by default), ordered by a bounding-box lower bound — read unmeasured_bound_mm before calling a pair the closest in the assembly. An overlap here is UNSIGNED, so wherever one node's box lies inside the other's the worker probes containment by ray parity: a contained pair is reported as an overlap with containment set, and one it could not decide (an open outer mesh) withholds the pass; pass is graded on bound_mm (min_mm less quantization_mm), and candidates left unmeasured beyond max_pairs whose box gap does not clear required_mm withhold it too. A declared overlap between references is excused, advisorily, only when FCL measured a penetration depth inside the allowance; with no depth it is never excused. minerva_cad_reference_profile {region_mm:{min_mm:[x,y], max_mm:[x,y]}, per_node?} answers the skin-height question over a footprint: the tallest reference geometry inside it, the node that owns it and the point that realises it, measured from the triangles clipped to the region. NEVER read a skin height off the node boxes in minerva_cad_references — a joystick node's box is 42 mm tall because of the stick while its housing is 10 mm, so an enclosure sized from the boxes grows to fit geometry that is not there. Those boxes — and the keep-out envelopes emit_dsl writes from them — answer the other question, what volume must stay CLEAR, where erring large is correct.
4e. expected_contacts — an assembled design touches itself ON PURPOSE: the keycap presses the actuator, the holder rests on the door, the collar locates the speaker, the board sits on its bosses. Graded against required_mm every one of those is a failure, so the top-level pass is unreachable and you end up reading fifty rows by hand. Declare them instead, on check_clearance and check_interference alike: expected_contacts:[{reference, node?, region_mm?, required_mm?, why?}]. NAMING A NODE IS USUALLY TOO COARSE — a board node carries both the bosses you meant to rest on and the traces nothing may touch — so add region_mm:{min_mm:[x,y,z], max_mm:[x,y,z]}, a world box the contact has to lie in; a contact on the same node outside it is graded as if you had declared nothing. required_mm is the gap that pair must keep instead of the call's own: 0 (the default) lets the surfaces touch, a positive value grades that pair to its own bar, a NEGATIVE value declares an interference fit that deep. A DECLARATION CANNOT HIDE A CRASH, and you should not want it to: overlap deeper than the declaration allows (0.01 mm by default) is reported and fails anyway, and an overlap the check found by ray parity — with no measured depth — is never excused. AN EXCLUSION IS CERTIFIED ONLY WHEN ITS EVIDENCE IS: the overlap depth the interference check measures is a chord along an edge, not an upper bound, and a region matches the one witness point of a distance measurement without measuring the pair outside it — so a declared overlap held inside its allowance and a region declaration are applied ADVISORILY (certified: false / ungraded_outside_region on the row, pass false with a pass_reason and advisory true on the reply, verdict 'advisory' in check_design). Only a declared pair measured at a positive GAP at or above its own required_mm is a certified exclusion; say 'advisory' when you report a design whose intended contacts overlap. Every declaration comes back in expected_contacts with the value measured for it, counted by excluded_count, and one that matched nothing is listed in expected_contacts_unmatched: check that list, because a declaration that stopped matching usually means the contact moved. Declare the contacts you designed, once, and then read `pass`.
4d. minerva_cad_check_fasteners {screw:{dia_mm, length_mm, head_dia_mm}} — will the screws actually go in? It pairs each bore in your solid with the reference hole it lines up with, one to one, and grades four things per screw: COAXIALITY as ISO 1101 states it (a cylindrical zone about the hole's axis that has to contain your bore's axis over the engaged length) against the radial slack an ISO 273 medium clearance hole gives that screw — an M3 passes a 3.4 mm hole, so it may wander 0.2 mm sideways and no more; PATH, a ray fan down the axis at the shank and head radii that names the node and the point of the first thing in the way — including the board's own hole wall when the hole is too small; ENGAGEMENT, the overlap of the screw's length from the seat with your bore, against 2.0 x d by default (thread-forming into plastic — pass engagement_min_d 1.0-1.5 for metal); and HEAD SEATING. Read axis_source on every row: b_rep is the exact OCCT axis, tessellation_fit means the kernel had no cylindrical face for that bore and the axis was fitted to the display mesh with tessellation_tolerance_mm of chordal error. The path check is SAMPLED, not swept: nothing narrower than ray_spacing_mm is guaranteed to be seen. SAY WHERE THE HEAD SEATS. screw.seat is 'reference' by default — the head lands on the plate the hole is in, which is the board-on-bosses case. For a two-shell enclosure — an M3 coming up from below through a counterbore in the tray floor, through the board, into a pilot in a post; or a screw through a lid into a boss of the base — pass seat:'solid' and the seat is measured as the first face of your own solid the head meets coming in; a board or a component in the way is then an obstruction, not a seat. Get this wrong and every axial number is off by the height of the stack: the row reads 'bottoming' on a joint that is fine. A coaxiality row with graded:false is not a failure: no ISO 273 medium entry exists for that size, so pass clearance_hole_dia_mm if you want it judged. Read `unpaired` too — a boss that matched no hole is usually the actual mistake, and the check will not invent a partner for it. Its solid features arrive as one row per diameter and fit, {dia_mm, count, indices}, because a shell has thirty of them and they never change; the indices are the solid_feature numbers a `pairs` override names, and detail="full" hands back the rows with their centres when you need to place one. Pairing prefers a bore the screw can THREAD into (narrower than its clearance hole) over one it only passes through, so a board sandwiched between a clearance bore in the tray and a pilot in the post above pairs with the pilot without being told; a row's bore_fit says which kind it got, and overlap with a 'clearance' bore is reported but is never engagement. When the pairing IS wrong anyway, override it with pairs:[{solid_feature, reference_hole}] — reference_hole is the `index` in the reply's reference_hole_index list, which is the check's own numbering (a hole with no usable axis never enters it, so it is not find_holes' order). Obstruction rows are collapsed to one per (node, span) with a `count` and the axial range the rays met it over: one rib met by forty rays is one row, not forty. `why` says in one sentence which of the four numbers to act on. head_seat_supported is ADVISORY: it is the fraction of the seat ring that landed on material, reported and not graded, so a head hanging over an edge does not fail the screw — read the number. ORIENTATION: a row always grades a hole in the REFERENCE against a bore in YOUR solid; screw.seat says which of the two the head lands on.

WHICH PART GETS CHECKED. By default all three checks read the part the document evaluates to — the last top-level assignment whose value is a 3D shape, or the shape a trailing bare expression names — and every reply says which, as `part`. So a two-part enclosure is checked in one pass when you bind the union last (part = bottom + lid), even though the halves do not touch; last_eval.body_count then reads 2, and a body_count you did not expect means the DSL made a body you did not mean to. To check named halves separately in one call, pass parts:["bottom", "top"]: each is evaluated as your document with that binding as its trailing expression and gets its own report under `parts`, with the call's `pass` true only when every part passed. THE ITERATION LOOP. On a document with a mesh() in it, one edit is: doc_write the new source -> read last_eval.interference (4b — it is already there, free) -> minerva_cad_check_clearance for the gaps that have to hold (4c) -> minerva_cad_check_fasteners for the joints (4d). Do all four before telling the user it fits. Interference alone passes a shell that misses the board by a hair and a screw that meets a capacitor; clearance alone passes a boss 0.5 mm off its hole. checked:false with a reason, from any of them, is a check that did not run — never report it as a pass.
5. minerva_cad_probe — turn a pixel of a snapshot into a position in millimetres.
5b. minerva_cad_get_selected_reference — what the user CLICKED. See §14.
6. minerva_cad_view_overlay then minerva_cad_snapshot — when you do want a picture, put a millimetre grid and the world axes in it first, and use the returned px_per_mm (orthographic panes only) to read it. For a picture of ONE thing rather than of the pane, minerva_cad_snapshot_fit frames a Perspective pane on the solid, a named reference or a world box so it fills the pixels — without moving the camera the owner is using.

Every position comes back in BOTH frames: {world, local}. `local` is the reference's own converted frame — millimetres and Z-up, with the mesh() pose taken back off. The file's own units and up-axis have already been applied, so these are the numbers you write into the DSL: the pose is already in the mesh() line. `world` is the posed scene — that is what you compare against the evaluated solid and against other references. Mixing them up puts geometry in the wrong place with no error message.

The first measurement on a newly loaded file does the segmentation and builds the colliders. The segmentation runs on a worker thread and the verb awaits it, so the app stays responsive while it runs; the collider build still runs on the main thread, and so does a ray-grid fallback at a fine pitch_mm — those two stall the app for their duration. On a very large mesh (a hundred thousand triangles or more) the first minerva_cad_find_holes or minerva_cad_find_cylinders can still take several seconds to answer. Warn the user before the first call on a big file, and pass `node` to segment one node instead of all of them. After that the result is cached until the file changes, so ask as many questions as you need; two verbs asking about one file at once share a single segmentation. Because a verb waits, the document can change under it: the verb then runs once more, and if the document is still changing the reply carries stale: true with a stale_reason — its numbers describe a pose the document no longer has, so call again once the edit has settled. Measurement never alters the reference, and there is no verb that cuts geometry against one — if the user wants a pocket that matches a scanned part, model it from the numbers you measured.

§4 — The user's click is your seed

A reference mesh has no names you and the user share. "This bracket", "that hole", "the tall post" mean nothing to a verb that takes a node name and a diameter. The panel's wide sidebar lists every reference and every node inside it, and a left click in any view selects the node under the cursor and the point on its surface. minerva_cad_get_selected_reference hands you exactly that: the reference, the node, the surface point in both frames, the node's bounds, and the fitted hole the point fell inside if it fell into one. A node is identified by its PATH from the file root ("Assembly/Bracket/Body"), because foreign assemblies reuse leaf names freely; every node= filter accepts either the path (one node) or the bare leaf name (every node carrying it), and a filter that matches nothing is an error listing the nodes there are.

When the user says "this" or "that" about a reference, read the selection FIRST. Then measure that node by name (every measurement verb takes `node`), and quote the numbers back with the node's name so the user can see you are looking at the same thing. If nothing is selected, the reply lists the mounted references — either ask the user to click, or use minerva_cad_select_reference to point at one yourself, which highlights it in their sidebar.

An annotation can be stuck to that point: the cad/point anchor stores the point in the reference's own frame, so re-posing the mesh() line moves every annotation on it, and deleting the line marks them stale instead of stranding them. Edge selection is untouched by any of this — edges belong to the evaluated solid, nodes belong to the references, and both selections stay set at once.
